summary:
The Astronaut Health Monitoring System is a web-based project developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It is designed to simulate the health monitoring of astronauts during space missions through a futuristic NASA-inspired dashboard.

The system displays important health parameters such as heart rate, blood oxygen level (SpO₂), body temperature, and blood pressure. It automatically generates simulated health readings at regular intervals and allows users to manually enter health data.

The dashboard analyzes the readings and classifies them as normal, warning, or critical based on predefined demonstration thresholds. It also displays alerts whenever abnormal readings are detected. A heart rate chart helps visualize health trends over time, while local storage maintains reading history in the browser.

Key Features:
- Real-time simulated health monitoring.
- Manual health data entry.
- Health status detection and alerts.
- Heart rate trend visualization.
- Reading history using local storage.
- Responsive and futuristic dashboard design.
details:
Our system continuously monitors an astronaut’s vital signs and flags early signs of health problems, without needing a doctor on board. A wearable device (a wrist band or chest patch) measures heart rate, blood oxygen (SpO₂), body temperature, respiration rate, and movement. The data goes wirelessly to a small onboard unit, which analyzes it in real time and compares it against the astronaut’s own baseline. If readings drift outside safe ranges, the system alerts the crew member and sends a summary to mission control. Everything is shown on a simple dashboard with live graphs and trend history.

Benefits

  • Detects problems early, such as cardiovascular strain, fatigue, or oxygen issues, before they become emergencies
  • Gives continuous, hands-free monitoring, so astronauts don’t have to stop work for manual checks
  • Personalized thresholds, since each person’s normal differs
  • Works with delayed or limited communication, because analysis happens on board rather than depending on Earth
  • Builds a long-term health record useful for research on spaceflight’s effects on the body

Intended impact

Long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars will put crews far from immediate medical help. We want to make space travel safer by giving astronauts and mission teams an early warning system and a clear picture of crew health over time. The same technology could also support remote patient monitoring, elderly care, and rural healthcare on Earth.

How it’s creative

  • It adapts to each astronaut, using a personal baseline instead of one-size-fits-all limits
  • It combines several signals to judge overall health, rather than reading each sensor alone
  • It is designed around the space environment: low power, compact, and able to run offline
  • Its dashboard is simple enough to read at a glance during a busy mission
  • The design applies naturally to healthcare on Earth, which gives it value beyond space

Factors our team consider

  • Microgravity: how it changes heart rate, blood flow, and sensor readings
  • Accuracy and reliability: sensors have to work under motion, vibration, and varying conditions
  • Power and size: low consumption and a lightweight, comfortable wearable
  • Communication delays: on-board processing so alerts don’t depend on a link to Earth
  • Privacy and data security: health data must be protected
  • Comfort and usability: the device must be easy to wear for long periods
  • Cost and scalability: affordable components and a design that can expand to a full crew
  • Safety: avoiding false alarms while never missing a real emergency
